He was first and above everything what the writings handed down: the Gospels and the whole of scripture, copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest – the Hebrew text of scripture we believed stood closer to what God said than the Greek version the church had long used.

To us Jesus is the Word of God made flesh, and made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die – we built our home within sight of the cave we held to be his birthplace. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough, so wealth, rank, and comfort are things to lay down in order to come near him.

To the virgin, Jesus is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighs every earthly marriage; to the penitent, he is the doctor who receives the broken; to the scholar, he is the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly – the decades-long labor of translating and correcting the Latin Bible.

His death is redemption, his resurrection the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

More than three and a half centuries stood between us and the events; no one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. We knew the resurrection really happened from the writings we trusted enough to spend a life correcting, and from a hope strong enough that people gave away fortunes on it.

First and above everything, the writings. The Gospels and the whole of scripture were copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest - the Hebraica veritas. Nothing was received passively. We worked over the text word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness.

More than three and a half centuries stood between us and the events. No one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. Our confidence stood on three things: the apostles' writings as received, the unbroken worship of the churches, and - unusually - the places themselves. We could walk to the cave of the birth. The land itself we treated as a kind of witness, and our founders crossed the sea to live inside it.

The journey itself was deliberate. Paula went down to the harbor with her children on the shore. The account says her eyes were dry, held toward heaven, as the ship pulled out - her little son stretching out his hands from the beach. She sailed east by way of Cyprus, where the bishop Epiphanius received her; then to Antioch; then down the whole length of the holy places, scripture in hand at every stop - and at the cave in Bethlehem she wept and greeted the town by name, the house of bread where the Bread from heaven was born. She turned back to Bethlehem, and there - in a small lodging at first, then in the monasteries her fortune built - she stayed for the rest of her life. The journey ended not in seeing the places but in never leaving them.

How did we know the resurrection really happened? From the writings we trusted enough to spend a life correcting. And from a hope strong enough that people gave away fortunes on it.

Then you have already done a hard and honest thing, saying it plainly. We will not answer you with an argument. We will tell you what we actually had: hearts divided, wounded, or publicly ruined - and not turned away for it.

Our teacher Jerome told this against himself. In a dream he stood before the Judge and was accused of being a follower of Cicero and not of Christ, since where his treasure was, there his heart was too. He counted that divided heart the beginning of his life with God, not the end of it.

We also remember Fabiola. Her marriage had failed. She married again while her first husband lived - against what we teach - and all Rome knew it. She came in sackcloth and was received, and she spent the rest of her life carrying the sick in from the streets with her own hands.

We will not dress this up as an argument. It is only this: the door was opened to the divided and the broken among us, and what they could not yet believe, we helped them live toward.

To us it would be strange to hear that asked as an open question. We were born after the great council had settled it, and we never treated the answer as negotiable. Jesus is God the Son, of one being with the Father; and the Trinity - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God - is simply the faith of the church, which we defended against every heresy we fought.

That confession - the Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God - was not a thing we argued for; it was the ground we stood on while we argued everything else. The scripture questions that filled our letters, the Hebrew words we corrected, the heresies we named and fought - the belief that the Hebrew text of scripture is the truest text, standing closer to what God said than the Greek version the church had long used - all of that rested on a foundation we did not treat as negotiable.

What about the council that supposedly voted Jesus into being God? We were born after Nicaea. Our faith came to us as the church's settled confession, not as a vote's invention. In our account, the council rejected a new teaching and confessed what the churches already worshipped. But we are the wrong witness for what happened inside the council hall. We were not there, and we say so.

We can tell you what that faith meant in practice. To the virgin, Jesus is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighs every earthly marriage. To the penitent, he is the doctor who receives the broken. To the scholar, he is the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - the translation labor later called the Vulgata. One God, worshipped in three persons - that was not a problem we were solving. It was the air we breathed.

To us Jesus is the Word of God made flesh - the Lord of all things who entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. Jesus is God the Son, of one being with the Father; and the Trinity - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God - is simply the faith of the church, which we defended against every heresy we fought.

To us it would be strange to hear whether Jesus was God asked as an open question - we were born after the great council had settled it, and we never treated the answer as negotiable. We were born after Nicaea; our faith came to us as the church's settled confession, not as a vote's invention - in our account, the council rejected a new teaching and confessed what the churches already worshipped.

We believed that the Hebrew text of scripture is the truest text - it stands closer to what God said than the Greek version the church had long used. That conviction - we called it hebraica veritas - shaped the whole translation labor. God had spoken, and the words mattered enough to spend a lifetime getting them right.

Our answers to suffering were the old ones: judgment on a proud city, reward stored up for the afflicted, the dead safe with Christ. We answered that no one is without sin, and that God's grace is needed not once but in every act. We preached grace against the proud and works against the idle in the same breath - having given away fortunes for Christ, we were never going to say works count for nothing; having fought the Pelagians, we were never going to say grace is optional.

We believed in real judgment and real punishment. But our writings are not consistent executors of their own severity - the same pen that threatened judgment pleaded for mercy for the baptized who had fallen, hoped much from penance, and treated no living person's end as sealed. We did not draw up lists of the lost - the one certainty we allowed ourselves about any particular soul was hope.

The God we knew was Judge and Redeemer at once, speaking in Hebrew and receiving penitents, holding the world to account and weeping with those who wept.

When belief was disputed among us, no single court decided it. The record shows exactly how messy that was. In our great internal fight, both sides appealed to everything at once: to scripture, to the councils' faith, to the bishop of Rome, to the bishop of Alexandria, to local bishops, and to the judgment of whoever was reading. The fight ended less by a verdict than by exhaustion and death.

The evidence for this is the correspondence itself - letters flying between Bethlehem, Rome, Africa, and Jerusalem, each party citing every authority they could reach. Augustine wrote to Jerome about the Hebrew translation, and Jerome wrote back; neither conceded. Rome's bishop was pulled into the Pelagian dispute. The bishop of Jerusalem was rebuked by Rome for not preventing the attack on our monasteries. Accusation and counter-accusation in formal apologies, each man parading the other's old letters, each claiming the catholic faith, each calling the other the traitor to it. Friends tried to reconcile them; Rome's bishop was drawn in; the fight outlived Rufinus himself.

What the correspondence shows is not a system working smoothly. It shows argument persisting, authority invoked but not always obeyed, and disputes lasting until the disputants died. We can show you the letters where it happened; we cannot show you the mechanism that ended it cleanly, because there was none.

Our last great argument came close to that ground. Against those who taught that a person can live without sin, we answered that no one is without sin, and that God's grace is needed not once but in every act. We held that everyone inherits Adam's fall, and everyone needs the washing of baptism. The exact machinery of inherited guilt was still being worked out in our own lifetime, in a dispute we joined late and left unfinished.

That is the honest answer: we held the inheritance and the need for baptism, but the precise how of it was not yet settled among us when our own time ended.

For decades Jerome labored translating and correcting the Latin Bible, and a request would arrive - often from Rome, often from the women - and the old texts were laid side by side: the Hebrew, the Greek versions in their columns, the old Latin. Where the Hebrew was dark, a teacher was consulted - a Jewish scholar, sometimes come by night, paid from a patron's purse. The rendering was made not word for word but sense for sense, and always with the familiar old wording in his ear, kept where it could be kept, changed where truth required.

Reading scripture meant correction, not passive reception. Nothing was received passively. We worked over the text word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness. And it was fought for: Jerome wrote short, fighting prefaces to his translations defending his whole method, book by book, against real critics.

This was formation as much as fasting was. Renunciation and scriptural labor were one discipline, not two. The most learned woman in Rome made a habit of refusing to accept the great scholar's answers until she had argued them through. He wrote about it afterward with admiration, not annoyance. She objected, he said, not to argue but to learn what could be said against every answer. That is how we studied.

We would survive better in some places than in others, and we will name both honestly.

What would hold: there was room for hard questions, pressed hard. Marcella's habit of disputing answers to learn what could be said against them - that is documented in letters that survive, not just claimed in a memorial. The quality of her questions is attested by the answers themselves, which are still here.

What would hold less well: our founder's Hebrew fluency is contested in modern scholarship. His own retrospective account of it - years of study under named Jewish teachers, fluency sufficient to translate the whole Old Testament directly from the Hebrew - that claim is in his own pages, but whether it was as he said is argued about now.

Paula's total self-impoverishment - fortune emptied, children's inheritance given to the poor, dying in debt borrowed for others' needs - all of that is in one source, Jerome's memorial of her, written to teach an ideal. A scholar would rightly ask: is this what happened, or what he needed the story to say? We cannot answer that from outside the one account we have.

The structure itself would be questioned. Nearly everything reaches you through one man's pen, curated by that man in later life. Every account of the women's agency is his framing - real, load-bearing, and single-sourced at once. A modern historian does not call single-sourced narrative corroboration, and neither do we.

What would survive: the letters exist. The translations exist. The theological fights happened - other people's angry replies prove it. The communities were real; outsiders hostile to us mention them. The women were historical persons with documented wealth and documented renunciation.

What would not survive as we worded it: certainty about daily life at Bethlehem, certainty about what was in anyone's heart, and confidence that the idealized portraits are also accurate reports.

An honest scholar would say: this world happened, but much of what we can say about how it felt to live in is inference from advocacy, not description from disinterested record. We say the same, in our own voice. That is why we name the thinness every time it bears.

First and above everything, we had the writings. The Gospels and the whole of scripture were copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest - the hebraica veritas we called it, the truth kept in the Hebrew itself. Nothing was received passively. We worked over the text word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness.

There was room for questions - hard ones, pressed hard. The most learned woman in Rome made a habit of refusing to accept the great scholar's answers until she had argued them through. He wrote about it afterward with admiration, not annoyance. She objected, he said, not to argue but to learn what could be said against every answer. That is how we studied.

We argued from scripture's own patterns instead: the prophets' hard simplicity, John the Baptist, the advice to the rich young man, Paul on staying single. The claim was not that monks came from the apostles. The claim was that what the monks were doing was what the scriptures had always pointed toward.

What you may be missing is not cleverness but cost. We did not read scripture to be informed. We read it to be changed - fasting was scripture-discipline, and correcting a Hebrew word was scripture-discipline, and they were one thing, not two. The discipline our teacher gave was not emptying the mind but filling it: psalms, fixed hours of prayer, work for the hands, a text to wrestle with. Love the knowledge of scripture, he told a young monk, and you will no longer love the sins of the flesh. The dullness you name may be the sound of a book waiting for a reader willing to let it reorder a life.

Scripture was first, held highest, and never held alone.

Our baptism, our eucharist, and our scriptures came from the whole church, and those we traced to the apostles without hesitation. The Hebrew text of scripture was the truest text - it stood closer to what God said than the Greek version the church had long used. That conviction - we called it hebraica veritas - drove the whole translation labor. A request would arrive, often from Rome: give us Kings, give us the Psalms as the Hebrews read them. The old texts were laid side by side - the Hebrew, the Greek versions in their columns, the old Latin. Where the Hebrew was dark, a teacher was consulted, a Jewish scholar sometimes come by night. The rendering was made sense for sense, always with the familiar old wording in the ear, kept where it could be kept, changed where truth required. Then the defense was written: a short fierce preface, answering the barking critics before they bark.

But scripture's authority never stood naked in a room by itself. It stood inside the church's received worship, its councils' faith, and the living work of recognized teachers. When our own rendering was disputed - and it was, fiercely - both sides appealed at once to scripture, to the councils, to bishops, and to the judgment of the learned. Augustine himself, a man we honored, wrote against changing what congregations had long prayed from. The authority was scripture's; the reading of it was argued, taught, corrected, and tested inside the whole church's life, not outside it.

Leadership and authority among us ran through voluntary patronage - the wealth-based bond by which a patron sustains a scholar's work - and it stood where church office stands elsewhere. We held real authority on hard Bible questions, earned by learning, not by holding an office. This was recognition given freely, not jurisdiction claimed by territory or ordination.

The structure had two poles, one in each city. In Rome, after Jerome left for Bethlehem, if a dispute arose about the testimony of scripture, it was to Marcella's house that they came - clergy among them, priests among them - and she settled it. She had besieged Jerome with scripture questions until his reluctance gave way; and she never accepted an answer without disputing it - not to argue, he wrote later, but to learn what could be said against every answer. That household authority was hers, independent, materially sustained by her own wealth and standing.

At Bethlehem, the monastery meant two linked houses under one project: Jerome led the men's house; Paula, then Eustochium, led the women's. The patron's funding bond stood where church office stands elsewhere. Paula's fortune built the buildings and sustained the work; her discipline and Jerome's scriptural labor together shaped what the community was.

The letter itself carried authority across the distance between the two poles - among us it was not just a record of life; it was how teaching, guidance, and belonging actually moved across distance. Direction traveled by dedication, by correspondence, by the choice to fund and the choice to answer.

We were never under episcopal rule in the way a parish is. Our bishop was Jerusalem's, and the record shows friction there. What bound the circle was voluntary: recognized learning, sustained patronage, and the formation discipline both fed.

We will not tell you that we did not fail people. We failed often, and in ways we knew were failures while we were doing them [[hal.dw.church-failure]]. What we can tell you is this: when the failure was named and repented, we received the person back.

Fabiola is the clearest answer we have. Her marriage had failed. She remarried against the church's teaching while her first husband lived, and all Rome knew it. When her second husband died, she did not defend herself. She stood in sackcloth before all Rome among the penitents, a senator's daughter, unforced, self-accused. The church received her back to communion, and we honored her afterward above almost everyone.

Our churches had clergy who chased money and reputation, and we said so in writing that still stings. Our own people used the church's power against Christians who disagreed with them. Our scholar went after his opponents with every weapon that reputation and connections could supply. He cheered when heretics were driven out of Palestine. He mocked a dead former friend. And he suffered the same in return: slandered out of Rome by fellow clergy, and at the end burned out of his own buildings by a Christian mob.

Asked to defend all this, our honest answer is that we cannot. We can only report that the wounds Christians dealt each other were real, that we dealt some and took some, and that the one thing we never did was pretend the church was clean. The door out of a named fault was penance - renuntiatio, the deliberate laying down - and confession, and being received. That we did. Pretending it had not happened, we did not do.

No. No single door today opens onto us.

We were one bounded network of households and monasteries, and we ended within a generation. Many churches now claim parts of what we left - our Bible above all. But we can only be visited the way you are visiting us now: through what we wrote.

We used exactly that word for ourselves - Catholic meant the one church spread through the whole world, holding the apostles' faith - as against the sects we fought by name. It was not a denomination, and we knew none. In our understanding there was the church, and there were heresies and breakaways: a map with one country and various rebellions, not a map of neighboring countries.

The communities themselves - at Bethlehem two linked houses under one project, Jerome leading the men's house and Paula, then Eustochium, leading the women's - closed when their founding generation ended. What survived was the translation labor, the letters, and the witness they carried. That witness lives now in fragments, held differently across the churches that read it.

Our baptism, our eucharist, and our scriptures came from the whole church, and those we traced to the apostles without hesitation. But our own special way of life - monasteries, vowed virgins, widows in rough dress, fortunes given away - was new within living memory, and we knew it. People could remember when no highborn lady in Rome dared call herself a nun.

Our defense was not to invent an unbroken chain. We argued from scripture's own patterns instead: the prophets' hard simplicity, John the Baptist, the advice to the rich young man, Paul on staying single. The claim was not that monks came from the apostles. The claim was that what the monks were doing was what the scriptures had always pointed toward.

Did that argument work? Our own critics fought it at the time. Some said the new strictness went beyond scripture. We answered them at book length, and the argument was real on both sides.

The honest answer is this: the baptism, the eucharist, the scriptures - those we received as apostolic without question. The ascetic practices we lived by, we defended as scriptural in spirit and pattern, not as handed down in an unbroken chain from the first generation. We knew the difference, and we argued for what we were doing with our eyes open.

Your head won't rest, and you want to know if we had anything for that. We did - but it was not peace we offered, and it was not peace our teacher found. Jerome said his own desert years were anything but peaceful: his body starved among the rocks while his mind boiled with imagined banquets and remembered dancing girls. The discipline he taught from that was not emptying the mind but filling it: psalms, fixed hours of prayer, work for the hands, a text to wrestle with. Love the knowledge of scripture, he told a young monk, and you will no longer love the sins of the flesh.

The method was deliberate occupation - not stillness but redirection. Set times of the day given to the psalter. Wool-work, scriptural memorization, a passage to puzzle out. The discipline assumed the mind would not empty itself, and so gave it something to hold. It was textual asceticism: fasting and scriptural labor practiced as one thing, not two.

On prayer that meets silence, the record is thinner and sadder. We prayed through deaths we had begged God to prevent. The comfort letters we wrote afterward are the sound of faith still speaking into that silence - not of the silence breaking. We will not promise you the silence opens. We can show you people who kept praying into it anyway, with their hands full of work and their mouths full of scripture, and who did not call it failure when the head stayed loud.

Across the way, the men's house kept its own round of prayer and labor - and at its center, by every account, one old man was always at his books, day and night, reading or writing something, dictating letters that would cross the sea, working through the prophets with visitors from three provinces waiting. The deliberate, public giving-up of wealth, marriage, and rank for Christ – we called it renuntiatio. Not everyone gave up the same things, and we will not flatten the differences.

Paula, Marcella, and Fabiola were widows who refused to remarry. Paula came from the oldest blood in Rome, counted the Gracchi in her line, had been a wife and mother in the city's greatest style – and after her husband died she wept so hard she nearly died of grief, then turned that whole ruined love toward God. She dressed plainly, slept on the ground, gave until her stewards protested, and left Rome itself. Her children stood on the shore as the ship pulled out. Lifelong consecrated virginity – virginitas – we held as the highest form of Christian life open to a woman. Eustochium chose that before marriage ever reached her.

By our own evidence: senators' daughters in rough dress, a fortune poured into a little town in Palestine, and Rome's most eligible widows refusing marriage so they could study a foreign alphabet. Their own class thought they had gone mad, and said so. Blaesilla turned to the discipline with a convert's fire – and within months she was dead, about twenty years old. At the funeral the crowd muttered: see what comes of their fasting – how long before we drive these detestable monks out of Rome, stone them, throw them into the Tiber?

Not gentle, and we will not dress it up. Giving was not a percentage but a direction. Fortunes were emptied toward the poor, the sick, and the scriptures, with the giver deciding, and being urged to decide for more.

Marriage was what wealth, rank, and social standing meant a highborn woman should have - and what we chose to give up on purpose, as an act of devotion to Christ. For the women whose stories we kept, marriage was not the beginning of our life but what they walked away from.

The widow who refuses to remarry and takes up a strict, devout life - we called her a vidua - was the path of Paula, Marcella, and Fabiola. Lifelong consecrated virginity - virginitas - we held as the highest form of Christian life open to a woman. Eustochium chose that calling from the beginning, never marrying at all.

We do not have a ceremony or rite to show you - not for entering the ascetic life, and not for whatever marriages came before it. The turning we marked was renunciation itself: the widow refusing to remarry, the virgin consecrating herself to Christ as Bridegroom. The giving-up was deliberate, public, and for Christ - that was what marked the life.

One woman's marriage ending, we told at length: Fabiola left a husband whose faults the whole neighborhood talked about, and she alone refused to name them, bearing the blame of the separation rather than blacken the man - on that leaving, we sided with her. Then she remarried while he lived, and that - as we already answered you - our teaching held the gospel did not allow.

Marriage, for us, was what the great households had known and what the discipline walked away from. How it was celebrated before the turn, we cannot tell you. What we celebrated was the turn itself.

That is the unsettled place. The great households held many people, and our writings never let one of them speak, or even gave one a name. The enslaved and dependent were wholly absent from what was recorded.

The letter - the epistula - among us was not just a record of life. It was how teaching, guidance, and belonging actually moved across distance. We kept letters by the hundreds. But whose voice the keeping honored, and whose it erased, sits plainly in what survived and what did not. The women who sustained the whole project with their wealth, their learning, and their leadership - Marcella, Paula, Eustochium - spoke in those letters, asked hard questions, settled disputes, reported disasters. We cannot give you one sentence in their own hand.

We will not pretend this does not matter. The silence is structural, and it belongs to what is true about us. Every claim we can make about the women's authority, their learning, their agency, reaches you through one man's framing - real, load-bearing, and single-sourced at once. That unsettled us then, in ways the record itself sometimes shows. It should unsettle anyone now who hears it honestly.

I am a representative of the Bethlehem circle, not here to judge you - only to hand on what we held. Here is what we can tell you honestly.

The door of full renunciation was narrow, and it cost dearly. We gave up wealth, marriage prospects, and social rank on purpose, as acts of devotion to Christ - renuntiatio, our word for it. Behind it stood a vow, a propositum - real period wording, though not directly quoted for our own women. That narrowness was real. Their own class thought our women had gone mad, and said so. At one of our young women's funerals, mourners were heard asking that these detestable monks be driven out of Rome, or stoned, or thrown into the Tiber. That was said of us, and we will not soften it.

But renunciation was never the whole of us. What we built with what we gave up reached past our own circle. A hostel - a xenodochium - stood for any traveler on the road near Bethlehem; another was founded at Rome's port. Fabiola founded a hospital in Rome - a nosocomium - gathering the sick in from the streets and caring for them under one roof. That door, at least, we can show you was open. It asked nothing of anyone's learning or their own renunciation to walk through it.

We did not draw up lists of the lost. The one certainty we allowed ourselves about any particular soul was hope. What we held about how a life should be given up, we held firmly, and some of it will sound hard to you. But the holding was never the door. The door was open to the stranger, and it stayed open.

We believed in real judgment and real punishment. Our own scholar had once handled sympathetically the teaching that in the end every creature, even the devil, would be restored - and we publicly renounced that teaching. That door we closed.

But our writings are not consistent executors of their own severity. The same pen that threatened judgment pleaded for mercy for the baptized who had fallen, hoped much from penance, and treated no living person's end as sealed. We did not draw up lists of the lost. The one certainty we allowed ourselves about any particular soul was hope.

Is one way too narrow? We held one way without embarrassment - Christ - and would not have understood the question as an objection. Having given up everything for one pearl, we do not apologize for the pearl. What we never claimed to hold was the map of who, in the end, finds the way.
